question: Should directors cut their films to temporary music borrowed from other scores?
answer: A temp track is the clearest brief a composer can get. Directors rarely have words for music, and a borrowed cue shows the tone, pace and weight a scene needs. Editors cut rhythm to it, and test audiences need some music to judge a film at all. Without it everyone guesses until the score arrives, too late to change the cut.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether a reference can stay only a reference.
counterpoint: Temp music becomes a cage. After weeks of hearing a borrowed cue, directors fall for it and ask composers for near-copies, which flattens scores into soundalikes of whatever was borrowed. The cut itself is shaped around someone else's phrasing, so any new music has to fit a mould. The composer is hired to be original, then paid to imitate.
reference: Kalinak, Film Music: A Very Short Introduction, Oxford University Press, 2010
